title: Uncle Tom or Smart-Ass: how Black players seek work
summary: Hall argues few Black jazz players learn to approach employers and that there is no middle ground.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: -- same office. I don't think -- I don't

think many Black jazz players are aggressive in the right direction as far as getting employment. It's an art that you have to learn along with playing the instrument, as to approach and what's expected of you and what you can do, how to go about it, et cetera. And definitely there are not enough guys that do that.
And I made a study of it. You wind up being called Smart-Ass.
So what are you going to be, an Uncle Tom or a Smart-Ass?

Yeah, that's, you know -- the Uncle Toms can make it because they're controlled. Yeah. And there are a lot of them, polished, but the inference is there, nevertheless. But go the other way and you're in trouble.
You don't think there's a middle ground --
You think there have been any periods where it got better for a person to be just a person?
It's always -- you think it's always just kind of got along that way.
It's the nature of this society?
Yeah, I guess it's the label that could be used for prejudice. It doesn't all have to do with ability.
